newsitem.title: USA: U.S., China cast WTO talks in positive light.
newsitem.headline: U.S., China cast WTO talks in positive light.

text.p: The United States and China sought on Tuesday to cast on-going talks on Beijing's entry into the World Trade Organization in a positive light.

"We believe there has been a constructive atmosphere," U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin told a news conference following a two-day meeting with Chinese economic policymakers. But, he added, "there is a lot of work to do."
For his part, Chinese Finance Minister Liu Zhongli took note of what he called the "flexible and pragmatic" attitude of the U.S. toward Chinese membership in the WTO.
China in the past has accused the United States of blocking its entry into the WTO, charging that Washington has set too high a standard for Beijing's membership in the trade group.

Officials from both sides discussed the WTO issue, among a wide range of other economic matters, at the two-day meeting of the U.S.-China Joint Economic Committee. However, no WTO negotiations were conducted.
Rubin called the meetings "highly valuable," and said another gathering of the committee might be held toward the end of next year in Beijing.
In a joint communique after the talks, Rubin and Liu announced a series of steps aimed at furthering economic cooperation between their two countries in the tax, securities and financial arenas.
Rubin said he expects China to approve "very shortly" the applications by foreign banks to conduct local currency business in Pudong, Shanghai, on a trial basis.
For his part, Liu said Beijing will issue licenses to foreign banks wishing to do business in China in the future according to the pace of economic development in the country.
Four U.S. banks currently have seven branches in China.
Liu also announced China's plans to achieve current account convertibility for its currency by year's end. Chinese officials have previously indicated their desire to achieve that goal.
Rubin also said that "good progress" had been made on the bid by Chinese banks to open branches in the United States, although nothing specific was agreed on.
Federal Reserve Governor Lawrence Lindsey attended the U.S.-China talks. The U.S. central bank is the agency responsible for approving the Chinese bank licenses.

In the joint communique, the two sides noted that Chinese banks' efforts to win licenses to operate in the United States would be helped by Beijing bringing its banking supervision in line with international standards.
The two sides are expected to meet again in the first quarter of next year to discuss financial services issues.
Speaking through an interpreter, Liu praised the United States for its unconditional renewal of most-favored-nation trade privileges for China over the past three years.
Under current law, the U.S. must reconsider China's MFN status every year.
Rubin said that a lot would need to happen before that law -- which covers other issues besides MFN -- could be changed to give China permanent trading privileges.
